newsitem.title: USA: Smart New Year money moves.
newsitem.headline: Smart New Year money moves.

text.p: What's the best financial posture for 1997?
Three themes come to mind: Protect, simplify and adapt.
Protect, because after 1996's rip-roaring market, you've more to lose when the floor falls away.
Simplify, because ... well, wasn't that one of your New Year's resolutions? Life is complicated enough.
And adapt, because last year Congress made 655 changes in the tax code alone, and there's more promised for this year.
Here are 10 simple moves that should leave you well positioned to enjoy the surprises 1997 will have to offer.

-- Weed your wallet. Three credit cards are more than enough. The best no-fee, low-rate card you can find; a separate card for business expenses; and, if you're willing to play the card game, a good rebate card. Those immediate 10 percent discounts for opening store cards were nice, but those private cards tend to have the worst terms and not be worth the wallet clutter. Don't just throw them away; cancel them in writing to keep your credit report pristine.

-- Rebalance your investments. Go back to the mix you figured was smart a year ago: some money in stocks, some in bonds, some in foreign securities. You'll probably have to pull some out of domestic stock funds and move money into foreign stocks and bonds to get back to proper balance. Don't overlook real estate investments, either. Just about every economist with a press release machine is predicting tough sailing for 1997; maybe they are right and maybe they aren't. But if you hold to a diversified mix of investments, you'll receive pleasing gains in good times and softer falls in bad times. Don't forget to rebalance your 401(k) investments.
-- Put at least one savings plan on autopilot. Authorise a mutual fund to tap your checking account for $50 or $100 or $500 a month. You really won't miss the money, and it will accumulate.

-- If you buy your own health insurance, revisit your policy. Many states have been passing their own health care reform legislation, and some policies are actually cheaper than they used to be. The federal law kicks in in July. Make sure that you don't buy into plans with low "per-illness" caps that could cut off care in a true catastrophe. If you are self-employed, or work for a small company that offers only catastrophic coverage, run, don't walk, to a provider which is offering Medical Savings Accounts. These are a congressional tax gift that may not last through 1997.

-- Review your mortgage and other home equity debt. Rates remain near historic lows. If you're paying more than 9 percent and intend to stay longer than two years, refinance. If you're paying more than 9 percent and intend to stay less time than that, look at an adjustable rate mortgage just to make sure you wouldn't save by refinancing.
-- If you're a housewife, get your own Individual Retirement Account. Congress says you can shelter $2,000 annually starting this year in a tax-deferred account.

-- Cut the expenses on your investments. Brokerage fees, high mutual fund management fees and more will really bite into returns once those returns come back to earth. If you like doing the work yourself, go for low-cost, no-load mutual funds. If you don't, find an adviser who will suggest a series of no-load, no-deferred-sales-charge funds for a flat fee, and then let you go out and buy them.

-- If you're old and rich, take the money and run. If you've amassed so much in your retirement accounts that your distributions top $150,000 a year, you can take as much as you want without worrying about that pesky 15 percent excess distributions tax. At least until the year 2000, when the provision waiving that tax expires. Since there's no waiver of the excise estate tax for pensions that are inherited, you might as well use it yourself.

-- Learn something new. Read up on why more investment advisers are recommending index mutual funds instead of actively managed funds. Get on the World Wide Web, and check out the many informative investment sites online. If you haven't done it yet, put your family finances on the computer.
-- Watch Congress like a hawk for changes in home-selling capital gains taxes and tuition tax breaks. And have a happy new year!
